Market Maps That Sales Actually Uses

The Commercial SystemPart 5

By lowob · 20 July 2026 · 9-minute read · Strategy

A market map that sales uses is not a slide. It is a list of named accounts held in the CRM, each with a segment, a tier, the trigger that makes it timely, an owner and a status, refreshed on a fixed rhythm. Most maps fail because they describe the market rather than direct the work. Gartner found 84% of sales leaders said analytics had less influence on sales performance than expected, and Forrester found sellers choosing from an average of 1,400 sales assets. Another document will not help. A working map turns the segment choice from Part 3 into a weekly list of who to call and why.

Every commercial team has a market map somewhere. Usually it was built for a board meeting or a fundraise: a grid of categories, logos in boxes, perhaps a total addressable market figure in the corner. It describes the market accurately. Nobody in sales opens it again.

That is not a failure of effort. It is a failure of form. Sellers work from lists, not landscapes. A map that cannot be filtered, assigned and updated in the system they already use competes with everything else on their screen, and loses. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently. A map that adds work will be ignored.

Why most market maps die in a slide deck

Five properties separate a map that is used from one that is admired.

PropertySlide mapWorking map
UnitCategories and logosNamed accounts with a record each
LocationA deck or a design fileThe CRM, as fields and views
OwnershipWhoever built itAn owner per account and an owner for the map
TimingA snapshotA trigger and status per account, refreshed monthly
ActionNone impliedA next step per tier

The analytics evidence explains why form matters. A Gartner survey of 303 sales leaders, reported in February 2024, found 84% said analytics had less influence on sales performance than expected, and recommended a decision-driven approach: start from the decision a seller has to make, not from the data available. Forrester's 2022 research found reps had an average of 1,400 sales assets to choose from. A market map built as one more asset joins that pile.

The layers of a working map

A working map has four layers. Each lives in the CRM or in a tool connected to it.

LayerContainsWhere it livesWho updates it
UniverseEvery account that meets the segment filters from Part 3Account records, tagged by segmentRevenue operations, quarterly
Fit and tierFit score, potential and tier for each accountAccount fieldsRevenue operations, with sales input, quarterly
TimingCurrent trigger, its date and sourceAccount field or activitySellers and data feeds, continuously
CoverageOwner, status, last meaningful contact, next stepAccount and activity recordsAccount owner, weekly

The universe should be finite and countable. If it holds 1,200 accounts, everyone should be able to see the same 1,200. That number also anchors the bottom-up sizing check in Part 3 (Segment selection with evidence).

Tiering the map

Tiers decide where effort goes. They should combine fit (how closely the account resembles customers who won, stayed and grew) with potential (the realistic value if it buys). Current spend is a weak proxy for either.

Gartner research reported in 2021 found that customers elevated to key-account status mainly for their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time, and that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed key-account quota. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found top performers prioritised accounts and personas they had successfully closed before. Fit, in other words, predicts better than size.

TierTypical share of the universeCriteriaCoverageMotion
Tier 15% to 10%High fit, high potentialNamed owner, account plan, multi-threadedAccount-based, with partner and executive involvement
Tier 220% to 30%High fit, moderate potential, or the reverseNamed owner, triggered outreachSignal-led sequences and events
Tier 3The restMeets segment filtersPooled or marketing-ledContent, partners and inbound
ExcludedRecorded separatelyFails a disqualifierNoneTaken only as a recorded exception

The shares are illustrative starting points, not benchmarks. What matters is that Tier 1 is small enough for each account to have a plan. The account-based approach for Tier 1 is covered in our explainer (What is account-based marketing?).

Triggers make the map timely

A tier says who matters. A trigger says why now. Without triggers, sellers work the map alphabetically or by habit.

A trigger is evidence that an account's commercial conditions have changed in a way that alters the likelihood, timing or value of a purchase: a regulatory deadline, a new executive, an expansion, a failed implementation, a contract renewal date. Our piece on signal-based outbound sets out how to score signals by recency, relevance, magnitude, access and proof (Signal-based outbound).

The evidence for timing is consistent. Ebsta found high-intent accounts closed at 3.4 times the velocity of others. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 73% actively avoided suppliers who sent irrelevant outreach. A trigger is what makes outreach relevant.

Trigger typeExampleSourceDecay
RegulatoryA rule with a compliance date that affects the accountRegulator publicationsSlow: months to the deadline
PeopleNew head of the buying functionPublic profiles, announcementsMedium: first 90 days matter most
CorporateExpansion, acquisition, new market entryFilings, pressMedium
TechnologyRetiring a system the offer replacesJob posts, partner intelligenceMedium
RelationshipContract renewal with a competitorPartners, past conversationsFast once the date passes

Record the trigger on the account with its date. A trigger older than its decay period should drop the account's priority automatically.

A tier says who matters. A trigger says why now. A map needs both to direct a week of work.

Whitespace and the installed base

Most market maps show only prospects. The installed base often holds faster revenue. A whitespace view lists each current customer against the offers the firm sells, and marks what each has bought, what it could buy and what it has declined.

McKinsey's 2021 analysis of B2B commercial analytics described a distributor that was losing customers representing up to 30% of its yearly sales and, by focusing analytics on churn first, added $5 million to $10 million in run-rate revenue within eight months. Gartner's account-growth research found organisations that frequently update account plans are three times more likely to build customer decision confidence.

Customer (illustrative)Core offerOffer BOffer CRenewal dateNext step
Account 1BoughtDeclined, 2025: budgetFit, not discussedQ2Introduce C with a reference
Account 2BoughtBoughtNot a fitQ4Renewal review
Account 3BoughtFit, in discussionFit, not discussedQ1Resolve B before renewal

Recording why an offer was declined, and when, is what lets the firm return at the right moment.

Keeping the map alive

Maps decay. People change jobs, companies are acquired and triggers expire. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete. A map built on that data will mislead unless it is maintained (What is CRM data hygiene?).

The maintenance rhythm is modest and fits the operating rhythm in Part 6.

CadenceTaskOwner
WeeklyUpdate status and next step on owned accountsAccount owners
MonthlyRefresh triggers; expire stale ones; review Tier 1 coverageRevenue operations and sales lead
QuarterlyRe-score fit and potential; re-tier; review exclusionsCommercial lead
AnnuallyRe-run segment selection against a year of outcomesLeadership

Every re-tiering is a decision. Recording who moved an account, why and with what expectation lets the firm test its tiering logic against outcomes later. This is also where the map meets The Build Order. A context layer can assemble an account brief from the CRM, email and filings in minutes (The context layer, followed through one account). It cannot tell a seller why the account is Tier 1 unless someone recorded the reason.

Illustrative example: from slide to CRM
Decision
Retire the market map slide and rebuild it as CRM fields: segment, tier, trigger with date, owner and status, with a saved view per seller.
Reason and owner
Sellers reported working from personal lists; only a minority of Tier 1 accounts had any logged contact in the previous quarter. Owned by the revenue operations lead; agreed with the head of sales.
What changed
The weekly pipeline meeting opens with Tier 1 coverage; triggers older than 90 days expire automatically; re-tiering requires a recorded reason.

Illustrative: a composite of a 150-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Build lists, not landscapes. A map sellers use is a set of named accounts in the CRM.
  • Tier on fit, not spend. Accounts that resemble customers who won and grew deserve the effort.
  • Add the trigger and its date. Timing is what turns a list into a week of work.
  • Map the installed base. Whitespace and declined offers, with reasons, are often the fastest revenue.
Gateway card

Before you hand the map to sales

  • A finite, countable account universe tagged by segment
  • Tier criteria written down, based on fit and potential
  • A trigger field with a date and a decay rule
  • An owner, status and next step on every Tier 1 and Tier 2 account
  • A whitespace view of current customers with declined offers recorded
  • A monthly refresh with a named owner

Common questions

What is a market map in sales?

A list of named accounts in a target market, organised by segment and tier, with the trigger, owner and status for each, held in the CRM so sellers can work from it.

How do you tier accounts for sales?

Combine fit (how closely an account resembles customers who won and stayed) with potential value. Keep Tier 1 small enough for each account to have a plan.

What is whitespace analysis?

A view of current customers against every offer the firm sells, showing what each has bought, what it could buy and what it has declined, with reasons and dates.

How often should a market map be updated?

Status weekly, triggers monthly, tiers quarterly and the segment choice annually.

Next move

Count the accounts in your target segment that have an owner, a tier and a dated trigger in the CRM today. If the answer is under half, rebuild the map there before adding any new data source.
